content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper focuses on the task of monocular visual odometery (VO) which estimates the 6DoF poses of each frame with monocular videos as input. 
In the paper, the author tries to address the problem of high computational cost and low accuracy of previous classic and learning-based VO/SLAM systems by using high-level features extracted from image patches for building correspondences as opposed to dense features from the whole image and sparse keypoints. 
Results show that the proposed method outperforms DROID-VO and ORB-SLAM in terms of accuracy on TARTAN AIR, EuRoC MAV, and ICL_NUIM datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
1. the idea of this paper is easy to understand 
2. the paper is ready to read 

Weakness:

1. Limited novelty. The biggest contribution of proposed method is the usage of images patches, but I don’t see how image patches can help reduce the computational cost and improve the accuracy of the VO task. To be precise, image patches can be used to reduce the computational cost by performing patch-wise matching for dense correspondences prediction, e.g., optical flow. However, in the paper, depths of image patches are reprojected directly to another image, so these is no need to worry about the matching cost. As for the contributions of recurrent iterative updates and differential bundle adjustments, since they are widely used in previous methods, e.g., BA-Net, DROID-SLAM, we can hardly say they are novelties of this paper.

2. Missing experiments of the running time comparisons. In the paper, the author emphasizes the high speed of the proposed method, but there are no comparisons of the running time with previous methods including the learning-based DROID and classic ORB-SLAM, DSO. Neither do we know why the proposed methods achieves such high speed. Is it from the feature extraction component or from the optimization part? Experiments of running time can provide us a deeper understanding of this paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The quality of the paper is fair
The clarity is fair. 
The novelty is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on strength and weakness, I tend to reject the paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a deep learning based approach for visual odometry (VO). Inspired by direct VO methods, the proposed pipeline operates on image patches for which deep features are extracted and then correlated with the features of the projected frames. Temporal information is utilized by 1D temporal convolution on the patch trajectories and soft aggregation of patch-frame pairs. A 2D flow vector together with a confidence are predicted to update the patch location in each frame. An optimization function is defined based on the prediction and is optimized by the final bundle adjustment (BA) layer which outputs updates to the patch depth and camera poses. The system is trained on synthetic data and its performance is demonstrated on public synthetic and real datasets. The method consumes reasonable GPU memory and runs in real time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- This work addresses several limitations of existing deep learning based VO methods. It avoids large computational cost and meanwhile provides better accuracy.
- By design, the method has a constant runtime.
- The system is trained purely on synthetic data and is shown to work well on real dataset.
- The ideas of utilizing temporal information and aggregating information of neighboring patch frame pairs are novel. Their effectiveness is demonstrated by ablation study.

Weakness:
- While it is a plus that the system can be trained solely on synthetic data and it works on real data, this also exposes some limitations of the proposed work. Both pose and flow supervisions are required for training, which are hard to get for real data and often can only be provided by synthetic datasets. Generalization of the method is only tested on one real dataset, which is quite limited. 
- The effectiveness of the predicted confidence weights is questionable. There is no quantitative evaluation. Many of the color coded confidence in Fig. 8 are rather counterintuitive. 

Other small issues:
- - It would be interesting to see the depth accuracy. Since synthetic datasets are used in the evaluation, it would be straightforward to add such evaluation and potentially also compare to other methods. 
- n, m are not used in Fig 3
- Page 4 bottom "for each each edge" -> for each edge
- Page 5 "frame aggregation where edges are neighbors if they connect to both the same source and destination frames": I am a bit confused as in this paper edge is considered to connect a patch to a frame.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is clearly presented.
- The provided video demonstrates how the system works in reality and code is provided for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the paper presents a novel pipeline that addresses some limitations of existing peer work. But due to the weaknesses listed above, my rating is borderline.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: A deep learning monocular visual odometer system is proposed.  A neural network is used to extract collection of patches form incoming frames.  A bundle adjustment network is also implemented that is used to correct odometer on the fly.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper makes some bold claims that their monocular visual SLAM system is far superior to existing systems, both deep learned and traditional however when the results are presented, in the only standard dataset used out of the 3 that were tested, the results are not superior for half the cases.   The network is also trained using a simulated dataset and then claims of generality are proposed that it extends to many real data sets however only 2 datasets were tested besides the simulated one and I only recognize the one dataset.
IF claims of generality are made, testing should have been done on more datasets, a good collection of available benchmark data sets are available at
https://sites.google.com/view/awesome-slam-datasets
I am a bit disappointed that there was not a deep dive into what makes these patch features so superior, what is exactly being captured, this would have been an interesting investigation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Many details are missing for reproducibility.  For example, a quote from the paper "a local window of keyframes", however we do not know what a local window is, how many frames.  Also the patch extractor "extracts a sparse collection of image patches", how are these chosen, details? The tracking of patches is done using a recurrent neural network, why a RNN?, why not a conventional tracker, what are the advantages?  
I argue that the network is overfit to the tartan air dataset and that is why this dataset is evaluated with positive results.  Why was the ICL-NUIM dataset used, this seems obscure (see previous comments)?  The results non the EUROC MAV dataset are the ones I most value and the results are good but not superior.  The results are a mixed bag of results for easy and difficult cases.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper essentially presents a new feature type to use for visual odometry.  The feature type is based on a learned patch detector.  There is no depth analysis of these patches and why for the simulated training data, it appears to perform well.  What are these patches.  The results for the only credible dataset the EUROC MAV dataset, the results are a mixed bag.  The other datasets are obscure including the simulated training data set.  There are many other VO datasets available that were ignored.  If generality is claimed as it is, then more testing is required and more in depth analysis is required.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a deep learning based approach for extracting and tracking patches in frames while estimating camera poses in a monocular visual odometry. It consists of two primary stages: (i) a residual network is used to extract descriptors of patches, and (ii) a recurrent network produces the flow of the patches while estimating the camera pose using a differential bundle adjustment module which learns to minimize the patch reprojection error. Using EuRoC drone and ICL-NUIM datasets, it shows 43%~64% lower average pose estimation error than some state-of-the-arts, e.g. DROID-SLAM, with around 60~100 fps of efficiency running on a high-level GPU.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The proposed monocular VO performs efficiently while giving accurate camera pose estimation.
Although the networks are trained on synthetic datasets, the paper uses real-world dataset sequences to show the generalization of the learned networks.

Weaknesses
One of the significant weaknesses is the motivation. Learning descriptors for point features and tracking them for pose estimation could also give impressive performances, e.g. GCNv2, and learning poses from photometric consistency, e.g. D3VO, even outperforms the proposed work in the EuRoC dataset. The authors use 1x1 patch in the ablation study in order to demonstrate the importance of using a patch over a feature is not convincing as using local context for the network to learn feature correlation is intuitively better than using only one pixel.
There are a lot of unclear descriptions, e.g. What are the roles of context features in the update operator? What are “frame” and “patch” feature maps? What are the indices in Equation (4)? These unclear statements prevent the reader from understanding how the proposed method works.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Both the abstract and the conclusion are not informative in terms of (i) what the novelty and key features of the proposed approach is, (ii) what benchmarks and prior work the paper is using, and (iii) to what extent does the paper improve in accuracy and speed.
The motivation of using patches for feature tracking and camera pose estimation is very weak. Learning descriptors for point features and tracking them for pose estimation could also give impressive performances, e.g. GCNv2, and learning poses from photometric consistency, e.g. D3VO, even outperforms the proposed work in the EuRoC dataset. The authors use 1x1 patch in the ablation study in order to demonstrate the importance of using a patch over a feature is not convincing as using local context for the network to learn feature correlation is intuitively better than using only one pixel.
There are a lot of unclear descriptions, e.g. What are the roles of context features in the update operator? What are “frame” and “patch” feature maps? What are the indices in Equation (4)? Why is 384 dimensions the size of the hidden state? Also for Figure 1, it is unclear what the authors tried to express from the bottom figure.
content.summary_of_the_review: There is not a sufficient comparison to the state-of-the-art. Also, clearer and detailed descriptions of the method and motivation have to be enhanced which are expected to be provided in the rebuttal.
